title: Fallback Channels
summary: Fallback channels are reserve communication paths that malicious software keeps in case the primary path fails, is blocked or starts drawing attention. A typical implant carries a list of destinations, protocols or mediums and walks down that list when a connection fails, when a domain is blocked or sinkholed, or when traffic volume crosses a threshold the operator wants to stay below. The design removes a single point of failure and also lets an operator split a large transfer across several paths. Defenders rarely see one dramatic event; instead they see repeated failed connections followed by success, one process contacting several unrelated destinations, generated domain patterns, or a host suddenly using an unusual protocol or port. Proxy logs, firewall and flow records, domain name resolution logs and endpoint network connection telemetry are the main sources. The discriminator is change over time: legitimate software keeps a small, stable set of endpoints, while a fallback design rotates through several.

beginner.definition: A fallback channel is a spare way for harmful software to talk to the person controlling it. The first way is called the main channel. If that way stops working, the software tries the next one on its list. This keeps the attacker in contact even when defenders block one route.
beginner.whyItMatters: If you block one address, the attacker may simply move to another. Data can also be sent in small parts across several routes to avoid size limits. This makes clean up harder, because the software may still be reachable. Network logs often show the failed attempts first, which is a useful clue.
howItWorks: The harmful program carries a list of backup addresses, ports or methods to try.
It first tries the main channel and waits a short time for a reply.
If nothing comes back, or the reply is blocked, it moves to the next entry.
It may switch method completely, for example from web requests to another service.
It can split a large upload across several channels to stay under alerting limits.
It repeats this cycle quietly, so the operator keeps control of the machine.
beginner.example: Imagine you plan to phone a friend every evening, but the line is often busy. So you agree on three backups: a mobile number, an email address, and a note left at a cafe. If the first call fails, you try the next. Your friend always knows where to look. A fallback channel works the same way for harmful software. Blocking one phone number does not end the conversation, because two more are waiting on the list.
takeaways: Blocking one address is not enough when the software holds a list of alternates.
Repeated failed connections followed by a success are a strong fallback signal.
Watch for one program talking to several unrelated destinations in a short time.

objectives: Define fallback channels and explain why implants are built to be resilient.
Describe the conditions that make malicious software switch to an alternate channel.
Identify the network and endpoint log sources that reveal channel switching.
Compare normal application endpoint behaviour with fallback style rotation.
Explain how data can be split across channels to avoid transfer thresholds.
